q: The founder of the Pala dynasty of Bengal was:
explain: Gopala (750-770 CE) founded the Pala dynasty in Bengal. The Palas were great patrons of Buddhism and built the famous Vikramashila University.

q: The Tolkappiyam, the oldest Tamil grammar work, was compiled by:
explain: Tolkappiyam was compiled by Tolkappiyar during the Third Sangam. It is the oldest surviving Tamil grammar text, covering phonology (Ezhutthiyal), words (Sollliyal), and meaning (Porulliyal).

q: Iltutmish is considered the true founder of the Delhi Sultanate because:
opts: Consolidated the Sultanate and got Caliph's recognition
explain: Iltutmish (1210–1236) got recognition from the Abbasid Caliph (Islamic legitimacy), introduced the iqta system (land revenue assignments for military service), completed the Qutb Minar (started by Aibak), and introduced silver tanka and copper jital coins.

q: The concept of 'Ahimsa' (non-violence) as a political tool was first applied by Gandhi in:
explain: Gandhi first applied non-violent resistance (Satyagraha) in South Africa (1906–1914) while fighting for the rights of Indian immigrants. This experience shaped his philosophy for India's independence struggle.

q: The Indus script is:
explain: The Indus script (Harappan script) remains undeciphered despite many attempts. It contains over 400 signs and was written right-to-left.

q: Which British commander is most associated with the recapture of Delhi from the rebels in September 1857?
explain: Brigadier-General John Nicholson led the decisive assault that led to the recapture of Delhi in September 1857, though he was mortally wounded in the process.

q: Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism, attained nirvana at:
explain: Mahavira attained nirvana (moksha) at Pawapuri (Bihar) in 527 BC.

q: The concept of 'Ahimsa' was first emphasized in:
explain: Ahimsa (non-violence) was most strongly and systematically emphasized in Jainism, especially by Mahavira. It became central to Jain philosophy.

q: The Chola local self-government included three types of assemblies. For Brahmin villages, it was called:
explain: Chola village assemblies: Sabha (for Brahmadeya/agrahara villages of Brahmin settlements), Ur (for non-Brahmin villages), Nagaram (for merchant settlements). Sabha had elected committees (variyams) — example from Uttaramerur inscription.

q: The Korean War ended with:
explain: The Korean War (1950-53) ended with an armistice (ceasefire) on 27 July 1953, technically leaving North and South Korea still at war. The DMZ (demilitarized zone) divides the peninsula.

q: Which was the first capital of the Mughal Empire in India?
explain: Agra was the first capital of the Mughal Empire in India. Babur established it after the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

q: The Constituent Assembly of India was set up under the:
explain: The Constituent Assembly of India was set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946). It first met on 9 December 1946 with Dr. Rajendra Prasad as its permanent chairman from 11 December 1946.

q: Samudragupta is often called the 'Napoleon of India' because:
opts: Conquered most of North India via military campaigns
He introduced a new law code
explain: Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE) is called the Napoleon of India by historian V.A. Smith for his extensive military conquests across North India and the Deccan. The Allahabad Pillar inscription (by Harishena) records his campaigns.

q: India's first nuclear test was conducted at:
explain: India conducted its first nuclear test (Smiling Buddha) at Pokhran, Rajasthan on 18 May 1974. Second nuclear tests (Pokhran-II/Operation Shakti) were conducted in May 1998.

q: Operation Blue Star (1984) was conducted at:
explain: Operation Blue Star (June 1984): Indian Army stormed the Golden Temple in Amritsar to remove Sikh separatist militants led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale. Led to Indira Gandhi's assassination.

q: Who founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) and what was its main purpose?
opts: Swami Vivekananda — combining spiritual practice with social service (education, healthcare for poor)
explain: Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) in Belur Math, Howrah. It combines Vedanta philosophy with humanitarian work — schools, hospitals, disaster relief. Inspired by his guru Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.

q: The INA (Indian National Army) was originally organised by:
opts: Mohan Singh (1942); reorganised by Bose in 1943
explain: INA was first organised by Captain Mohan Singh from Indian POWs captured by Japan in Malaya (1942). Subhas Chandra Bose took over leadership in 1943, reorganised it, declared Provisional Government of Free India, and launched the Imphal-Kohima offensive.

q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place in:
explain: On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi day), General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, killing hundreds. This shocked India and changed the independence movement.

q: The Pandya kingdom's capital was:
explain: The Pandya kingdom's capital was Madurai (also called 'Koodal'). Pandyas ruled southern Tamil Nadu from Madurai. Megasthenes mentions Pandyas ruled by a woman (queen). They traded with Greeks and Romans.

q: The Kalinga War was fought by Ashoka in approximately:
explain: The Kalinga War (261 BCE) was fought between Ashoka and the state of Kalinga (modern Odisha). The enormous bloodshed (100,000 killed) led Ashoka to adopt Buddhism and non-violence.

q: The British East India Company was established in:
explain: The British East India Company (EIC) was established on 31 December 1600 by a Royal Charter of Queen Elizabeth I to trade with the East Indies. It began as a trading company and gradually became a ruling power.

q: The first battle between Indian rulers and Mahmud of Ghazni was at:
explain: Mahmud of Ghazni's first major battle in India was the Battle of Waihind (near Peshawar) in 1001 CE against Raja Jaipal of Punjab, whom Mahmud defeated.

q: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) defeated the:
opts: Shakas (Western Kshatrapas) of Malwa and Gujarat
explain: Chandragupta II (c. 375–415 CE) defeated the Shakas (Western Kshatrapas) of western India, annexing Malwa, Gujarat, and Kathiawar. This extended Gupta empire to the Arabian Sea. He took the title 'Vikramaditya'.

q:
Consider the following statements about the Harappan economy:
1. Standardised weights and measures based on a binary system have been found.
2. Evidence of trade with Mesopotamia exists in the form of Harappan seals found there.
3. Coined currency was used for internal and external trade.
4. Bronze tools indicate knowledge of alloying copper and tin.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — standardised weights, Mesopotamian trade evidence (seals found at Ur etc.), and bronze/alloying knowledge are all well-attested. Statement 3 is incorrect — no coined currency existed; trade was via barter. Hence only three.

q: Harshavardhana's court poet was:
explain: Banabhatta was the court poet of Harshavardhana. He wrote 'Harshacharita' (biography of Harsha).

q: The first cotton textile mill in India was established at:
explain: India's first modern cotton textile mill was established in Bombay in 1854 by Cowasjee Nanabhoy Davar. This marked the beginning of modern industrialization in India.

q: The Kailash Temple at Ellora is carved out of a single rock and was built by:
explain: The magnificent Kailash Temple (Cave 16) at Ellora was built by Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century CE) — carved from top to bottom out of a single basalt cliff, largest such structure in the world.

q: Fatehpur Sikri was built by:
explain: Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri (near Agra) as his new capital in 1571, named after Sufi saint Salim Chishti.

q: Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) was established by:
explain: Akbar established Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 CE for religious debates among scholars of different faiths — precursor to his Din-i-Ilahi.

q: 'Dhammachakkapavattana Sutta' refers to:
explain: Dhammachakkapavattana Sutta is the record of Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath (Deer Park) to his five former companions — the 'Setting in Motion of the Wheel of Dharma'.

q: The ancient Roman settlement found in Tamil Nadu is:
explain: Arikamedu (near Puducherry) was an ancient Roman trading settlement (1st century BCE - 2nd century CE) where Roman pottery, amphorae, and glass were found.

q: The first session of Indian National Congress was presided over by:
explain: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee (W.C. Bonnerjee) presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress in Bombay (December 1885).

q:
With reference to Neolithic settlements in India, consider the following statements:
1. Mehrgarh (in present-day Balochistan, Pakistan) shows some of the earliest evidence of farming in South Asia.
2. Burzahom in Kashmir shows evidence of pit-dwellings and domestic dogs buried with owners.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — Mehrgarh is one of the earliest farming sites in South Asia, and Burzahom (Kashmir) is well known for pit-dwellings and dog burials alongside humans.

q: The Dandi March (Salt March) of 1930 was:
opts: Gandhi's salt march from Sabarmati to Dandi (1930)
A march against the Rowlatt Act
A march to demand complete independence
explain: The Salt March (12 March – 6 April 1930): Gandhi led 78 followers on a 241-mile (385 km) march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to make salt from seawater, defying the Salt Laws. This launched the Civil Disobedience Movement — thousands were arrested.

q: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal primarily:
explain: Though Lord Curzon cited administrative efficiency, the partition of Bengal (1905) was primarily designed to break the unity of nationalist movements by creating Hindu and Muslim-majority provinces.

q: The Greek ambassador Megasthenes visited the court of:
explain: Megasthenes (c. 350–290 BCE) was the Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus I Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya. His account 'Indica' (mostly lost, known through fragments) described Mauryan India.

q: The first Tirthankara of Jainism is:
explain: Rishabhadeva (Adinatha) is the first Tirthankara (ford-maker) of Jainism. There are 24 Tirthankaras in total.

q: 'Swaraj Party' was formed by:
explain: Swaraj Party was formed in 1923 by C.R. Das (Deshbandhu) and Motilal Nehru, after disagreements within Congress on entering legislatures to 'wreck' the government from within.

q: The Nehru Report (1928) was drafted by:
explain: Nehru Report (1928) was prepared by a committee under Motilal Nehru (father), responding to the Simon Commission's challenge to Indians to draft their own constitution.

q: The Rowlatt Act (1919) was controversial because:
opts: Allowed detention without trial for up to 2 years
explain: The Rowlatt Act (Black Act) allowed the government to imprison any person suspected of terrorism for up to 2 years without trial. Gandhi called for a hartal (strike) against it, which led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

q: E.V. Ramasamy Periyar (Thanthai Periyar) founded:
opts: Indian National Congress — Tamil Nadu unit
explain: E.V. Ramasamy Periyar (1879–1973) founded the Self-Respect Movement (Suyamariyathai Iyakkam) in 1925 to fight against Brahminical dominance and caste system, and the Dravidar Kazhagam (DK) in 1944. He advocated rationalism, equality, and Tamil identity.

q: 'Narasimhavarman I' was also known as:
explain: Narasimhavarman I (630-668 CE) was called Mamalla (Great Wrestler) for his wrestling skills. The port city Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) is named after him.

q: Fa-Hien (Faxian) visited India during whose reign?
explain: Fa-Hien (399-414 CE), the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim, visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) to collect Buddhist scriptures and study Buddhism.

q: Market reforms during Delhi Sultanate were introduced by:
explain: Alauddin Khalji introduced market/price control reforms to maintain a large, cheap army.

q: The Industrial Revolution began in:
explain: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain (c. 1760–1840), driven by coal, iron, steam power, and textile innovations (Spinning Jenny, power loom, steam engine by James Watt). Britain's colonial empire provided raw materials and markets.

q:
Consider the following statements about the Cabinet Mission (1946):
1. It proposed a three-tier federal structure grouping provinces into sections.
2. It rejected the demand for a separate sovereign state of Pakistan at that time.
3. Differences between Congress and the Muslim League over 'grouping' contributed to its ultimate failure.
4. It resulted in the immediate transfer of full power to an elected Indian government in 1946 itself.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is incorrect — full transfer of power came only in August 1947 with independence and partition, not immediately in 1946. Hence only three.

q: Who presided over the Constituent Assembly?
explain: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Constituent Assembly.

q: The first battle of Tarain (1191) was fought between:
opts: Prithviraj III and Mahmud of Ghazni
explain: First Battle of Tarain (1191): Prithviraj Chahamana (Chauhan) defeated Muhammad Ghori. Second Battle (1192): Ghori defeated and killed Prithviraj, opening the way for Muslim rule in India.

q:
Consider the following statements about historians' interpretations of the Revolt of 1857:
1. V.D. Savarkar termed it 'The Indian War of Independence'.
2. Many British contemporaries dismissed it merely as a 'Sepoy Mutiny'.
3. The revolt saw active, wide-scale participation from the emerging Indian industrial working class.
4. Peasants and some civilian groups participated alongside sepoys in several regions.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — India's industrial working class was negligible/non-existent in 1857 (industrialisation had barely begun); participation instead came from peasants, some zamindars, and disbanded soldiers. Hence only three.

q:
Statement-I: The Moderates and Extremists within the Indian National Congress differed sharply on methods of political struggle before 1907.
Statement-II: Moderates favoured constitutional agitation and petitions, while Extremists advocated boycott, Swadeshi and more assertive mass mobilisation.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are correct, and the methodological difference described in Statement-II is exactly what constituted the sharp divide referred to in Statement-I, culminating in the 1907 Surat split.

q: The 'Ain-i-Akbari' was written by:
explain: Ain-i-Akbari (Institutes of Akbar) was written by Abul Fazl, Akbar's court historian. It is the third volume of Akbarnama, providing detailed accounts of Akbar's administration, policies, and the Mughal court.

q: Neolithic settlements in South India are found mainly in:
opts: River valleys of the Gangetic plain
The Deccan Plateau (Karnataka, AP, Tamil Nadu)
explain: Neolithic cultures in South India (c. 3000–1000 BCE) are found on the Deccan Plateau — sites like Brahmagiri (Karnataka), Piklihal, Utnur, Maski, Hallur. They used stone axes and kept cattle.

q: The Taj Mahal was built by which Mughal emperor?
explain: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra (1632–1653) in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: The division of the INC into Moderates and Extremists occurred at the:
explain: The Surat Split (1907) at the Surat session: Moderates (led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale) favoured constitutional methods; Extremists (led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak) demanded Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, and National Education.

q: The capital of the early Chola kings during Sangam age was:
explain: Uraiyur (near Tiruchirappalli) was the early Chola capital. Kaveripattanam (Puhar/Poompuhar) was their port city.

q: The Battle of Talikota (1565) resulted in:
opts: Destruction of the Vijayanagara Empire by the combined Deccan Sultanates
explain: At Talikota, the combined forces of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, and Golconda defeated Vijayanagara and razed the capital Hampi. This ended the Vijayanagara Empire's dominance.

q: The Meenakshi Amman Temple at Madurai was mainly built by:
explain: The Meenakshi Amman Temple in its present form was largely built during Tirumalai Nayak's rule (1623-1659 CE), though the temple itself dates back to much earlier Pandya times.

q: The Sangam-age port of Arikamedu (near Pondicherry) was excavated by:
explain: Arikamedu (ancient Poduke/Podouke) was excavated by Sir Mortimer Wheeler in 1945. It revealed a major Roman trading station with Arretine pottery, amphorae, glass, and gems — confirming active Indo-Roman trade.

q: Which Harappan city had a distinct 'lower town' and 'upper citadel' structure?
explain: Both Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had the pattern of a fortified citadel (upper town) and a lower residential town. Dholavira is unique for its three-part division: citadel, middle town, and lower town.

q: The Government of India Act 1935 introduced:
opts: Provincial autonomy and dyarchy at center
explain: Government of India Act 1935 introduced provincial autonomy (provinces got self-government), dyarchy at the Center, and established the framework for a federal structure — largely formed the basis of India's Constitution.

q: The States Reorganisation Act (1956) reorganised Indian states based on:
explain: The States Reorganisation Act 1956 reorganised Indian states based on linguistic lines, following the Fazl Ali Commission recommendations. 14 states and 6 Union Territories were created. Andhra Pradesh (1953) was the first linguistic state, formed for Telugu speakers.

q: Harappa was excavated for the first time by:
explain: Harappa was first excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921. Mohenjo-daro was excavated by R.D. Banerji in 1922. Sir John Marshall was the Director General of ASI who coordinated the excavations.

q:
Statement-I: The Harappans practised a largely egalitarian urban planning with a grid pattern and covered drainage system.
Statement-II: No large palaces or temples attributable to a ruling elite have been conclusively identified at major Harappan sites.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are factually correct — grid-pattern planning and drainage are well documented, and no unambiguous palace/temple has been identified. However, Statement-II does not directly explain Statement-I (the planning is inferred from urban layout itself, not from the absence of palaces); they are independently true facts.

q: Which Ashokan edict describes his conversion to Buddhism?
explain: The Bhabru (Calcutta-Bairat) edict mentions Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism and his faith in the Triple Jewel (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha).

q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) occurred because:
opts: General Dyer's troops fired on an unarmed crowd at Amritsar
It was a planned revolt by revolutionaries
explain: On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi), thousands gathered at Jallianwala Bagh (walled garden), Amritsar, to protest the Rowlatt Act. General Dyer ordered troops to fire without warning — killing ~379 (official) to 1,000+ (unofficial). This caused worldwide outrage.

q: Akbar's policy of 'Sulh-i-Kul' means:
explain: Sulh-i-Kul means 'universal peace' - Akbar's policy of religious tolerance and harmony.

q: The Constituent Assembly adopted the National Flag on:
explain: The National Flag of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947, three weeks before independence. The horizontal tricolor with Ashoka Chakra replaced the INC flag.

q: The First World War was also known as:
explain: World War I (1914-1918) was contemporaneously called 'The Great War' or 'The War to End All Wars'. The name 'World War I' became common only after the Second World War began.

q: The Sangam age in Tamil Nadu is generally dated:
explain: The Sangam Age (300 BCE to 300 CE) is the early classical period of Tamil civilization known from Sangam literature — a corpus of poetry by hundreds of Tamil poets.

q: The Rashtrakutas were the successors of:
explain: Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukya ruler Kirtivarman II and established the Rashtrakuta dynasty in 753 CE, making them the major power in the Deccan.

q: The Chola naval expedition against the Srivijaya Empire (Southeast Asia) was conducted by:
explain: Rajendra I led a successful naval expedition (1025 CE) against Srivijaya (Malay Peninsula and Sumatra), making Cholas the dominant naval power in Southeast Asia.

q:
With reference to early British economic policy in India, consider the following statements:
1. The Ryotwari system, introduced in parts of Madras and Bombay Presidencies, settled revenue directly with the cultivator.
2. The Mahalwari system, used in parts of North India, settled revenue with the village community.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — Ryotwari (Madras/Bombay, associated with Munro/Read) settled with individual cultivators, and Mahalwari (North-Western Provinces, Punjab) settled with the village/mahal as a unit.

q: The Gandhara art style was a blend of:
explain: Gandhara art (1st–5th century CE) blended Hellenistic/Greek realism with Buddhist iconography. It emerged in the Gandhara region (Afghanistan/Pakistan). First human images of the Buddha were made here.

q: The Battle of Khanwa (1527) was between:
explain: Battle of Khanwa (17 March 1527): Babur defeated Rana Sanga (Rana Sangram Singh) of Mewar, who had formed a coalition of Rajput chiefs to challenge Babur.

q: Bal Gangadhar Tilak gave the slogan:
explain: 'Swarajya is my birthright and I shall have it' was the famous slogan of Bal Gangadhar Tilak, the fiery nationalist who also started the Ganapati and Shivaji festivals for national awakening.

q: The Gupta period mathematician who wrote 'Aryabhatiya' was:
explain: Aryabhata (476–550 CE) wrote Aryabhatiya at age 23, containing mathematics and astronomy. He calculated pi ≈ 3.1416, explained solar eclipses, calculated Earth's rotation, and may have used a place-value system.

q: Sher Shah Suri is famous for:
opts: Grand Trunk Road, land revenue reforms, and the silver rupee
explain: Sher Shah Suri (1540–1545) defeated Humayun, reorganised the empire: Grand Trunk Road (Peshawar to Bengal), silver rupee (precursor to modern rupee), land revenue based on measurement (zabt), relay postal system, and built Sher Shah mosque.

q: The immediate cause of the 1857 revolt:
explain: The immediate cause was the introduction of Enfield rifle cartridges greased with pig and cow fat, offending Muslim and Hindu sepoys.

q: The British East India Company was founded in:
explain: British East India Company was established in 1600 by Royal Charter from Queen Elizabeth I.

q: Todar Mal was the Finance Minister of:
explain: Raja Todar Mal was Akbar's revenue minister who introduced the Zabti (measurement) system of land revenue — measuring land and fixing revenue based on soil type and cultivation.

q: The Arya Samaj was founded by Dayananda Saraswati in:
explain: Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay (1875). It advocated return to Vedic religion, rejected idol worship, caste by birth, and child marriage. It also started the Shuddhi (reconversion) movement.

q: The 'Din-i-Ilahi' was founded by:
explain: Din-i-Ilahi (Divine Faith) was founded by Akbar in 1582 CE — a syncretic religious movement incorporating elements of Hinduism, Islam, Zoroastrianism, Jainism, and Christianity.

q: Rajendra I's campaign to North India is commemorated by:
explain: Rajendra I (1014-1044 CE) launched an expedition to the Ganges and built a new capital Gangaikonda Cholapuram with its magnificent Gangaikondacholisvara temple.

q:
With reference to decolonisation after World War II, consider the following statements:
1. India gained independence from British rule in 1947.
2. Most African nations gained independence primarily during the 1950s-60s wave of decolonisation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — India's 1947 independence and the broader African decolonisation wave of the 1950s-60s are well-established historical facts.

q: The Nayanmars and Alvars were devotees of:
explain: Nayanmars (63 Tamil Shaiva saints) were devotees of Shiva. Alvars (12 Tamil Vaishnava saints) were devotees of Vishnu. Both composed devotional poetry (6th-9th centuries).

q: The Indian Councils Act 1861 was significant because:
opts: Introduced portfolio system; Indians nominated to councils
explain: Indian Councils Act 1861: introduced the portfolio system (individual ministers in charge of departments), allowed non-official (including Indian) members to be nominated to legislative councils, and allowed Viceroy to issue ordinances.

q: The Lucknow Pact (1916) was signed between:
explain: Lucknow Pact (1916) was signed between INC and Muslim League (proposed by M.A. Jinnah), agreeing on a common scheme for constitutional reforms and Hindu-Muslim unity.

q: The 1857 revolt was called 'First War of Indian Independence' by:
explain: V.D. Savarkar in his book '1857: The Indian War of Independence' (1909) called the 1857 revolt the First War of Independence, as it was organized resistance to British rule.

q: The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) proposed:
opts: Federal Union with provinces and groups
explain: Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) proposed a Federal Union of India with three groups (A, B, C) of provinces.

q: The epic 'Silappadikaram' was written by:
explain: Silappadikaram (The Story of the Anklet) was written by Ilango Adigal, believed to be the brother of Chera king Senguttuvan. It tells the story of Kovalan and Kannagi. It is one of the five great Tamil epics.

q: Muhammad bin Qasim invaded Sindh in:
explain: Arab commander Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 711 AD, the first Islamic conquest in the Indian subcontinent.

q: The Round Table Conferences (1930–32) were held in:
explain: Three Round Table Conferences were held in London (1930, 1931, 1932) to discuss constitutional reforms for India. Gandhi attended only the second (1931). They eventually led to the Government of India Act, 1935.

q: The 'Travels of Ibn Battuta' provides information about India during:
explain: Ibn Battuta (Moroccan traveler) visited India during Muhammad bin Tughluq's reign (1333-47 CE). His travelogue 'Rihla' gives detailed description of 14th century India.

q: Akbar's 'Sulh-i-Kul' policy means:
explain: Sulh-i-Kul (Peace with all/Absolute peace) was Akbar's policy of universal tolerance — treating all religions equally, respecting all faiths without discrimination.

q: Great Bath was found at which Harappan site?
explain: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro (11.88m×7.01m) is the most striking feature of the Indus Valley Civilization, used for ritualistic bathing.

q: The Pali Canon (Tripitaka) consists of:
explain: Pali Canon (Tripitaka = Three Baskets): Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules), Sutta Pitaka (discourses), Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophical analysis).

q: The Mauryan Empire declined after Ashoka mainly because of:
explain: After Ashoka's death (232 BCE), weak successors, heavy expenditure on Buddhist welfare, and weakening of military led to rapid decline. Pusyamitra Sunga killed last Mauryan king in 185 BCE.

q: 'Sati' was abolished by law under:
explain: Lord William Bentinck abolished the practice of Sati (widow self-immolation) by Regulation XVII in 1829, largely influenced by Raja Ram Mohan Roy's campaign.

q: The famous Tamil Vaishnavite saint who wrote 'Tiruppavai' was:
explain: Andal (Kothai) was the only female Alvar and composed Tiruppavai (30 verses, sung in Margazhi month) and Nachiyar Tirumozhi (143 verses). She is said to have merged with Vishnu at Srirangam (Ranganathaswamy Temple).

q: The immediate cause of the 1857 Revolt was:
opts: Cartridges greased with animal fat for the new Enfield rifle
explain: The immediate trigger was the introduction of the Enfield rifle cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, offending both Hindu and Muslim soldiers who had to bite off the cartridge tip.

q: The Tabaqat-i-Nasiri was written by:
explain: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri by Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani (1260 CE) is a valuable source of history of early Delhi Sultans, covering rulers up to Balban's period.

q: The policy of 'Blood and Iron' (despotism) was followed by:
explain: Balban (1266–1287) followed the policy of 'Blood and Iron' (loh-o-khalid) — ruthless suppression of rebellion, strict court discipline, Persian concept of kingship (Zil-i-illahi = Shadow of God), and separation of military from revenue departments.

q: Panchsheel Principles were signed between India and:
explain: Panchsheel (Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence) was an agreement signed between India and China on 29 April 1954.

q: Which Mughal emperor translated the Ramayana and Mahabharata into Persian?
explain: Akbar had the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and other Sanskrit texts translated into Persian, making them accessible to Persian-speaking scholars and promoting cultural synthesis.

q: Akbar's policy of 'Sulh-i-Kul' (Universal Peace) meant:
opts: Religious tolerance for all faiths (abolished jizya)
explain: Sulh-i-Kul was Akbar's (1556–1605) policy of universal harmony — abolishing jizya (non-Muslim tax), allowing free practice of all religions, marrying Rajput princess Jodha Bai, including Hindus in court, and starting Din-i-Ilahi (1582).

q: The Chola administrative unit 'Nadu' was governed by:
opts: A viceroy appointed by the king
explain: Chola administration: Empire → Mandalams (provinces) → Valanadus → Nadus → Urs (villages). Each Nadu was governed by Nattar (assembly of local landowners). The Cholas had a sophisticated system of village self-governance.

q: Triratna of Jainism refers to:
opts: Right Faith, Right Knowledge, Right Conduct
explain: Jain Triratna (Three Jewels): Right Faith (Samyak Darshan), Right Knowledge (Samyak Jnana), Right Conduct (Samyak Charitra) — the path to liberation.

q:
Statement-I: Buddhist stupas typically contain relics and are circumambulated by devotees as an act of worship.
Statement-II: The practice of circumambulation (pradakshina) around a sacred structure is unique to Buddhism and not found in Hinduism or Jainism.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Statement-I is correct — stupas hold relics and are circumambulated. Statement-II is incorrect — pradakshina/circumambulation is also a standard practice in Hindu and Jain temple worship, not unique to Buddhism.

q:
Consider the following statements about Indian temple architecture styles:
1. The Nagara style is predominantly found in North India and features a curvilinear shikhara.
2. The Dravida style is predominantly found in South India and features a pyramidal vimana.
3. The Vesara style is a hybrid seen in the Deccan region, e.g., under the Hoysalas and Chalukyas.
4. All Indian temples, regardless of region, strictly follow only the Nagara style.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — these are the three standard classifications of Indian temple architecture. Statement 4 is incorrect and contradicts 1-3. Hence only three.

q: The Cripps Mission (1942) promised:
explain: Cripps Mission offered Dominion Status to India after World War II, which was rejected by Congress and Muslim League.

q: 'Pallava Grantha' script is an ancestor of:
explain: Pallava Grantha script influenced the development of many Southeast Asian scripts including Thai, Khmer, Burmese, and Javanese, spread through trade and religion.

q: Shivaji Maharaj founded the Maratha Empire. His guerrilla warfare strategy was called:
explain: Shivaji's guerrilla warfare strategy was known as 'Ganimi Kawa' - swift raid-and-retreat tactics.

q: The epic 'Manimekalai' was written by:
explain: Manimekalai was written by Sithalai Sattanar (a Buddhist poet). It is the sequel to Silappadikaram, dealing with the adventures of Kannagi's granddaughter Manimekalai, who becomes a Buddhist nun.

q: Father of the Indian Constitution:
explain: B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee and is called the Father of the Indian Constitution.

q: Emergency in India was declared in:
explain: Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared the Emergency on 25 June 1975 (citing internal disturbance), lasting until 21 March 1977. Civil liberties were suspended and press censored.

q: The Gulf War (1991) was triggered by:
explain: The First Gulf War (1990-91) was triggered by Iraq's invasion and annexation of Kuwait (2 August 1990). A US-led coalition liberated Kuwait in Operation Desert Storm.

q: Bal Gangadhar Tilak's famous saying was:
opts: 'Give me blood and I will give you freedom'
'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'
explain: Bal Gangadhar Tilak's famous declaration 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' inspired the extremist nationalism. He used festivals (Ganesh Chaturthi, Shivaji Jayanti) to spread the freedom movement.

q: Who wrote 'Arthashastra', a treatise on statecraft and economic policy?
explain: Arthashastra was written by Chanakya (Kautilya), the chief minister of Chandragupta Maurya. It is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy.

q: Who presided over the Lahore session of INC (1929) that declared Purna Swaraj?
explain: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore session of INC (December 1929) where the resolution for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) was adopted, leading to the Civil Disobedience Movement.

q: The 'Quit India Movement' was launched on:
explain: The Quit India Movement was launched by Mahatma Gandhi on 8 August 1942 at the Bombay session of the All India Congress Committee with the slogan 'Do or Die'.

q: The Allahabad Pillar inscription records the conquests of:
explain: The Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayagraj), composed by Harishena (court poet), records the military campaigns and diplomatic achievements of Samudragupta and is called the 'Poem of Samudragupta'. He is often called the 'Napoleon of India'.

q: Permanent Settlement was introduced by:
explain: Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793) by Lord Cornwallis fixed land revenue permanently with zamindars, who became permanent owners of land if they paid fixed revenue.

q: Kabir was a disciple of:
explain: Kabir was a disciple of Ramananda. His poetry emphasized unity of God and rejected caste discrimination.

q: The 'Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms' of 1919 introduced which concept in Indian administration?
explain: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act 1919) introduced 'Dyarchy' in provinces — dividing subjects into 'transferred' (under Indian ministers) and 'reserved' (under the Governor) categories.

q: The Kalinga War, which is said to have caused Ashoka's turn towards Buddhism and the policy of Dhamma, is described in which of his edicts?
explain: Major Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga War and its aftermath, including Ashoka's remorse and turn to Dhamma.

q: 'Pattupattu' refers to:
explain: Pattupattu (Ten Idylls) are 10 longer Sangam poems, distinct from the Eight Anthologies, covering topics from love to war to nature.

q: Which of the following statements about the Indus Valley script is correct?
opts: It is written left to right
It is identical to Brahmi script
explain: The Indus/Harappan script remains undeciphered. Studies suggest it was written boustrophedon (alternating directions) or right to left. Over 400 signs have been identified. No bilingual inscription like Rosetta Stone has been found.

id: history-237-The first metal to be us
q: The first metal to be used by humans was:
explain: Copper was the first metal used by humans, followed by Bronze (alloy of copper and tin). The Bronze Age succeeded the Copper Age (Chalcolithic Age).

q: 'Kamban Ramayanam' (Tamil Ramayana) was written during the reign of:
explain: Kambar wrote the Tamil Ramayana (Iramavataram) around 12th century CE during the later Chola period, supported by a local chieftain Sadaiyappa Vallal.

q: The Poona Pact (1932) was signed between:
explain: Poona Pact (September 1932): Gandhi fasted unto death against Communal Award's separate electorate for untouchables. Ambedkar and Gandhi signed the pact — reserved seats within joint electorates instead.

q: The greatest Kushana ruler who patronised Buddhism was:
explain: Kanishka I (c. 127–150 CE) was the greatest Kushana emperor. He convened the 4th Buddhist Council in Kashmir, patronised Mahayana Buddhism, and his empire stretched from Central Asia to Pataliputra.

q: The Mahalwari system was mainly introduced in:
explain: Mahalwari system (introduced by Holt Mackenzie, 1822) fixed land revenue with the village community (mahal) collectively in North-Western Provinces (UP) and Punjab.

q: The Indus Valley Civilization is also known as:
explain: The Indus Valley Civilization is also called Harappan Civilization, named after Harappa — one of its major sites (in present-day Pakistan), excavated in 1921.

q: The Vedas are written in which language?
explain: The Vedas (Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda) are the oldest Hindu scriptures, written in Sanskrit. The Rigveda is the oldest, composed around 1500 BCE.

q: The Poligar Wars in Tamil Nadu were fought against:
explain: Poligar Wars (Palayakkarar Wars, 1799-1805) — South Tamil Nadu's local chieftains (Poligars/Palayakkarars) fought the British East India Company for their independence.

q: Who was the first ruler of the Maurya Empire?
explain: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 321 BCE with the help of Chanakya (Kautilya).

q: The Sangam Age in Tamil history refers to:
explain: The Sangam Age (approximately 3rd BCE–3rd CE) is a classical period of Tamil history named after the Tamil literary academies (Sangams). The three ruling families were Chera, Chola, and Pandya.

q: Who founded the Indian National Congress in 1885?
explain: Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant, founded the Indian National Congress in 1885 in Bombay. Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee was its first president.

q: The greatest Chola emperor who built the Brihadeeswara (Peruvudaiyar) Temple at Thanjavur was:
explain: Rajaraja I (985–1014 CE) built the Brihadeeswara Temple (Peruvudaiyar Kovil) at Thanjavur — a masterpiece of Dravidian architecture (UNESCO World Heritage Site). He also built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Gangaikondacholapuram.

q: The Banabhatta was the court poet of:
explain: Banabhatta was the court poet of King Harshavardhana (606-647 CE) and wrote Harshacharita (biography of Harsha) and Kadambari (prose romance).

q: The Maratha capital was:
explain: Shivaji's capital was Raigad Fort (Maharashtra). After his death, Satara became the seat of the Chhatrapatis. The Peshwas (Prime Ministers) ruled from Pune (Shaniwarwada palace).

q: Chandragupta II was also known as:
explain: Chandragupta II (375-415 CE) was known as Vikramaditya (Sun of Valor). His reign is considered the golden age of Gupta empire — Kalidasa, Varahamihira flourished in his court.

q: 'Tolkappiyam' is a grammatical treatise on:
explain: Tolkappiyam by Tolkappiyar is the oldest surviving work in Tamil literature — a comprehensive grammar covering phonology, word formation, and poetics. Part of early Sangam literature.

q: Mahatma Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in:
explain: Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920 in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and Rowlatt Act.

q: Jainism was founded by:
explain: Jainism's last and 24th Tirthankara is Vardhamana Mahavira (6th century BCE). He preached non-violence (ahimsa), truth, and non-possession. Jains believe in no creator god.

q: The integration of Hyderabad with India (Operation Polo/Police Action) was led by:
explain: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (Iron Man of India) directed Operation Polo (13–17 September 1948) — police action against the Nizam of Hyderabad who refused to join India. Major General J.N. Chaudhuri led the military action.

q: The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of:
explain: Fa-Hien (Faxian) visited India (399–414 CE) during Chandragupta II's reign. He described a prosperous, peaceful society, absence of capital punishment, and abundant food. He came to collect Buddhist scriptures.

q:
Statement-I: The Quit India Movement (1942) saw large-scale, spontaneous popular participation despite the arrest of top Congress leadership.
Statement-II: With Gandhi and other senior leaders arrested almost immediately, local leaders and ordinary people organised parallel governments and underground resistance in several regions.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are correct — the leaderless, spontaneous character of the movement (Statement-I) is directly explained by the mass arrests and consequent local/underground organisation described in Statement-II (e.g., the Ballia and Satara parallel governments).

q: Muhammad bin Tughluq's transfer of capital from Delhi to Daulatabad was:
explain: Muhammad bin Tughluq (1327 CE) transferred the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri) in the Deccan for better control of the empire, but it failed — the northern areas became unmanageable.

q:
With reference to the French Revolution (1789), consider the following statements:
1. It began with the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789.
2. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was adopted in 1789.
3. Louis XVI was executed in 1793 during the radical phase of the Revolution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are standard, well-established facts of the French Revolution. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: The Chola king who completed the construction of Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur:
explain: Rajaraja Chola I (985-1014 CE) built the magnificent Brihadisvara (Peruvudaiyar Kovil) Temple at Thanjavur, completed in 1010 CE. Also called Rajarajesvaram.

q: The Vedic period in India is characterized by:
explain: The Vedic period (1500-500 BC) is characterized by the composition of the four Vedas (Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda).

q: The 'Poona Pact' (1932) was signed between Gandhi and:
explain: The Poona Pact (September 1932) was signed between Gandhi (who was fasting unto death) and B.R. Ambedkar. It abandoned separate electorates for Depressed Classes (Dalits) in exchange for reserved seats in general electorates — increasing reserved seats from 71 to 147.

q: Sangam Age Tamil literature mentions foreign trade with:
explain: Sangam literature mentions extensive trade with Rome and Greece — export of spices, pearls, cotton; import of wine, gold, horses. Roman coins found at Arikamedu and other Tamil sites.

q: The Roman trade with the Sangam period Tamil kingdoms is evidenced by:
opts: Roman coins found in Tamil Nadu sites
explain: Roman gold coins (many dating to Augustus, Tiberius) found at Vellalur (near Coimbatore), Karur, Arikamedu (near Puducherry, a Roman trading post), and other Tamil sites confirm extensive Roman-Tamil trade.

q: The ancient city of Mohenjo-daro is located in present-day:
explain: Mohenjo-daro is located in Sindh province of present-day Pakistan. It was one of the major centres of the Indus Valley Civilization.

q: The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) proposed:
opts: A three-tier federal structure with united India (no partition)
explain: The Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946) proposed keeping India united under a loose three-tier federation: All-India Union, Groups of provinces, and Individual provinces with maximum autonomy. It tried to prevent partition but ultimately failed.

q: Sree Narayana Guru was a social reformer from:
explain: Sree Narayana Guru (1856-1928) was a great social reformer from Kerala who fought against caste discrimination. His famous saying: 'One Caste, One Religion, One God for Man'.

q:
Statement-I: The partition of India in 1947 was accompanied by large-scale communal violence and one of the largest mass migrations in human history.
Statement-II: The Radcliffe Line, drawn hastily to divide Punjab and Bengal, left many communities on the 'wrong' side of the new border.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are correct, and the hasty, ill-informed border demarcation described in Statement-II (the Radcliffe Line) is a primary reason for the mass displacement and violence described in Statement-I.

q: The First Battle of Panipat (1526) was fought between:
explain: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), establishing the Mughal Empire in India. Babur used artillery and flanking tactics to defeat Lodi's larger army.

q: Tipu Sultan was the ruler of which kingdom?
explain: Tipu Sultan (1750–1799) was the Sultan of Mysore. He was called the 'Tiger of Mysore' for his fierce resistance against British expansion. He died in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

q: Vasco da Gama first arrived in India at:
explain: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode, Kerala) in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to India.

q: Amar Jawan Jyoti is located at:
explain: Amar Jawan Jyoti (eternal flame) is located at India Gate, New Delhi, as a memorial for Indian soldiers.

q: 'Bande Mataram' was composed by:
explain: Bande Mataram was composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1870s, first appearing in his novel Anandamath (1882). It became the rallying song of the independence movement.

q: The States Reorganization Act (1956) reorganized states primarily on the basis of:
explain: States Reorganization Act 1956, based on the Fazl Ali Commission report, reorganized Indian states primarily on linguistic basis, creating 14 states and 6 Union Territories.

q: First round table conference was held in:
explain: First Round Table Conference was held in London in 1930 (Gandhi did not attend).

q: Mahavira attained 'Kaivalya' (enlightenment) at:
explain: Mahavira attained Kaivalya (perfect knowledge) at Jrimbhikagrama on the banks of Rijupalika river after 12.5 years of intense meditation.

q:
With reference to the integration of princely states, consider the following statements:
1. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with V.P. Menon, secured accession of most princely states by August 1947.
2. Junagadh's accession to India followed a plebiscite held in February 1948.
3. Hyderabad was integrated into India through 'Operation Polo', a military action in September 1948.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct — Patel and Menon's efforts, the Junagadh plebiscite (Feb 1948), and Operation Polo in Hyderabad (Sept 1948) are all well-documented. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: Mahavira attained Nirvana (Moksha) at:
explain: Mahavira attained Nirvana at Pawapuri (Pavapuri) in Bihar at the age of 72 (527 BCE). He was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali. He attained Kevala Jnana (omniscience) at Jrimbhikagrama.

q: The Great Wall of China was built primarily to protect against:
explain: The Great Wall of China was built over centuries, primarily to protect Chinese states and empires against Xiongnu nomadic tribes from the north — later associated with Mongol invasions.

q:
Match List-I (Mughal emperor) with List-II (associated event/policy) and select the correct answer:

List-I
A. Akbar
B. Jahangir
C. Shah Jahan
D. Aurangzeb

List-II
1. Reimposition of Jizya tax
2. Din-i-Ilahi and Mansabdari system
3. Construction of the Taj Mahal
4. Signed a farman granting trading rights to the English East India Company
explain: Akbar introduced Din-i-Ilahi and the Mansabdari system; Jahangir granted the English East India Company trading rights via farman; Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal; Aurangzeb reimposed the Jizya tax. Correct: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1.

q: The Pala dynasty was known for patronizing:
explain: The Pala rulers of Bengal (8th-12th centuries) were great patrons of Buddhism and Tantric art. They built Vikramashila University and sent Buddhist missionaries to Tibet.

q:
Match List-I (monument/site) with List-II (architectural style/period) and select the correct answer:

List-I
A. Sanchi Stupa
B. Kailasa Temple, Ellora
C. Konark Sun Temple
D. Qutb Minar

List-II
1. Rock-cut, Rashtrakuta period
2. Mauryan-Shunga stupa architecture
3. Kalinga temple architecture
4. Indo-Islamic (Slave dynasty)
explain: Sanchi Stupa (Mauryan-Shunga); Kailasa Temple Ellora (rock-cut, Rashtrakuta); Konark Sun Temple (Kalinga style, Eastern Ganga dynasty); Qutb Minar (Indo-Islamic, begun under Qutb-ud-din Aibak). Correct: A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4.

q: World War I was triggered by:
opts: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo
explain: WWI (1914–1918) was triggered by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (heir to Austria-Hungary) by Gavrilo Princip (Serbian nationalist) in Sarajevo, Bosnia. This set off the alliance system and led to a global conflict.

q:
With reference to Kashmir's accession to India, consider the following statements:
1. Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947.
2. The accession was triggered by a tribal invasion from Pakistan into Kashmir.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947, prompted by the tribal invasion backed by Pakistan that began in October 1947.

id: history-5-Ashoka was a ruler of wh
q: Ashoka was a ruler of which empire?
explain: Ashoka the Great (268–232 BCE) was the third emperor of the Mauryan Empire. He converted to Buddhism after the Kalinga War and spread Buddhist teachings across Asia.

q: The Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted because:
explain: The Simon Commission (led by Sir John Simon) had no Indian members, which was seen as an insult. Indians boycotted it with 'Simon Go Back' protests. It led to the Nehru Report (1928) as an Indian alternative.

q: Buddha attained enlightenment (Nirvana/Bodhi) at:
explain: Siddhartha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya (formerly Uruvela/Gaya), Bihar, under the Peepal tree (Bodhi tree) on the bank of the Niranjana river at the age of 35.

q: The Indian National Army trials (INA trials, 1945) were held at:
explain: The INA trials were held at Red Fort, Delhi (November 1945), charging INA officers with treason against the British. The trials created massive public outrage that unified Indians.

q:
Consider the following statements on India's post-independence economic planning:
1. The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 to formulate Five-Year Plans.
2. The First Five-Year Plan (1951-56) prioritised agriculture and irrigation.
3. The Second Five-Year Plan, based on the Mahalanobis model, emphasised heavy industry.
4. India adopted a fully market-driven, plan-free economy from 1951 onward.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is incorrect — India followed a mixed-economy, planned-development model (via the Planning Commission and Five-Year Plans) from 1951, not a market-only approach. Hence only three.

q: The battle that finally ended Maratha power was:
explain: Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18) battles of Kirkee, Korgaon, and Sitabaldi ended Maratha power. The Peshwai was abolished, Peshwa Baji Rao II exiled, making British supreme in India.

q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred in:
explain: Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, ordered by Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer.

q: The Pallava king who defeated the Chalukya king Pulakesi II was:
explain: Narasimhavarman I defeated Chalukya king Pulakesi II (who had previously defeated Harshavardhana) in 642 CE. He captured the Chalukya capital Vatapi and took the title 'Vatapikonda' (conqueror of Vatapi).

q: The Vedic age is broadly divided into Early Vedic (Rigvedic) and Later Vedic. The Later Vedic age is associated with:
opts: Agriculture, caste system, and large kingdoms
explain: The Later Vedic period saw settled agriculture, expansion eastward to Ganga plain, formation of 16 Mahajanapadas (great kingdoms), hardening of the varna (caste) system, and composition of Upanishads.

q:
With reference to the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22), consider the following statements:
1. It was launched by Gandhi in response to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the Khilafat issue.
2. It involved the surrender of government titles, boycott of schools, courts and foreign goods.
3. Gandhi called off the movement after the Chauri Chaura incident in 1922.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct — Jallianwala Bagh and Khilafat as triggers, the specific forms of non-cooperation, and the Chauri Chaura-triggered withdrawal (February 1922) are standard well-documented facts. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: The Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed:
explain: Rowlatt Act (March 1919) allowed the British to imprison anyone suspected of sedition without trial. Gandhi called for its withdrawal and launched a hartal (nationwide strike).

q: The word 'Arya' in Sanskrit means:
explain: 'Arya' in Sanskrit means noble, honorable, or respectable. It was a cultural/social term, not a racial one.

q: The Vijayanagara Empire's capital city was:
explain: The Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE) had its capital at Hampi (Vijayanagara) on the banks of the Tungabhadra river in Karnataka. It was a major centre of Hindu culture and the Kannada language.

q: The Tirukkural is divided into three sections called:
explain: Tirukkural by Tiruvalluvar is divided into: Aram (Virtue/Dharma), Porul (Wealth/Polity), Inbam (Love/Pleasure) — 133 chapters, 1330 couplets.

q: After the 1857 revolt, India came under:
explain: After the 1857 revolt, the Government of India Act 1858 transferred power from the East India Company to the British Crown. Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876.

q: Who was the author of 'Baburnama'?
explain: Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi) was written by Babur himself in Chagatai Turkish — it is the first autobiography in Islamic literary tradition, describing his life, campaigns, and observations of India.

q:
With reference to the Delhi Sultanate, consider the following statements:
1. The Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty was founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak.
2. Iltutmish is credited with organising the 'Iqta' system of land administration.
3. The Khalji dynasty introduced market-control (price control) reforms under Alauddin Khalji.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct — Aibak founded the Mamluk dynasty; Iltutmish organised the Iqta system; Alauddin Khalji's market reforms (price control on grain, cloth etc.) are well documented by Ziauddin Barani. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: The 1857 revolt started at:
explain: The 1857 revolt (First War of Indian Independence) began at Meerut on 10 May 1857.

q: The Partition of Bengal (1905) was ordered by:
explain: Lord Curzon ordered the Partition of Bengal on 16 October 1905, dividing it into East Bengal (Muslim majority) and West Bengal. This sparked the Swadeshi Movement and 'Boycott' agitation.

q: Who wrote Abhijnana Shakuntalam?
explain: Abhijnana Shakuntalam is a Sanskrit play written by the great poet Kalidasa during the Gupta period.

q: The 'Great Bath' was found at which Indus Valley site?
explain: The Great Bath was found at Mohenjo-daro. It is considered one of the world's first public water tanks and may have been used for ritual bathing.

q: Tukaram's compositions are called:
explain: Tukaram's compositions are called Abhangas — devotional poems addressed to Lord Vitthal (Vishnu) of Pandharpur. They are in Marathi and form part of the Varkari tradition.

q: The Treaty of Allahabad (1765), by which the Mughal emperor granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha to the East India Company, was signed between Robert Clive and which Mughal ruler?
explain: The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) was signed between Robert Clive and Emperor Shah Alam II, granting the Diwani rights to the Company.

q:
Match List-I (event) with List-II (year) and select the correct answer:

List-I
A. Partition of Bengal
B. Formation of Muslim League
C. Congress split at Surat
D. Formation of Home Rule League (Annie Besant)

List-II
1. 1906
2. 1907
3. 1905
4. 1916
explain: Partition of Bengal (1905); Muslim League founded (1906, Dacca); Surat split between Moderates and Extremists (1907); Annie Besant's Home Rule League (1916). Correct: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4.

q: Rani Lakshmibai was the queen of:
explain: Rani Lakshmibai was the queen of Jhansi, a heroic leader of the 1857 revolt.

q: The Hathigumpha inscription (in Odisha) mentions a powerful king named:
explain: The Hathigumpha inscription (carved in a cave in Udayagiri, Odisha) records the deeds of Kharavela, king of the Kalinga (Chedi) dynasty, around 1st century BCE. It is an important source for post-Mauryan history.

q: Who was the first Indian Governor-General of free India?
explain: C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) was the first and only Indian Governor-General of India (1948-1950), succeeding Lord Mountbatten.

q:
With reference to Indian classical dance forms, consider the following statements:
1. Bharatanatyam originated in Tamil Nadu and is traditionally associated with temple dance (Devadasi tradition).
2. Kathakali is a classical dance-drama form of Kerala, known for elaborate costumes and facial make-up.
3. Odissi originated in Punjab and draws heavily from Sikh devotional traditions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — Odissi originated in Odisha, not Punjab, and draws from Jagannath temple traditions, not Sikh devotional traditions. Hence 1 and 2 only.

q: The Swadeshi Movement (1905) involved:
opts: Boycotting British goods, promoting Indian-made goods
explain: The Swadeshi Movement arose after the Partition of Bengal (1905). It involved: burning foreign cloth, boycotting British goods, promoting Indian industries (Swadeshi), national schools, and Swadesh Sanghas. Leaders: Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai (Lal-Bal-Pal), Aurobindo.

q: The French Revolution began in:
explain: The French Revolution began in 1789 with the storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789). It overthrew the monarchy and established principles of Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.

q: Mirabai (Meera) was a devotee of:
explain: Mirabai (16th century Rajput princess) was an ardent devotee of Lord Krishna. She composed beautiful bhajans in Rajasthani/Braj Bhasha expressing her love for Krishna.

q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was launched in:
explain: Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in September 1920 (announced at Calcutta session of INC) calling for boycott of British goods, courts, and legislatures.

q: Which Pandya king is mentioned in the Ashokan edicts as a southern border king?
explain: Ashoka's Rock Edict II mentions 'the Pandyas' as southern neighbors where Ashoka's dharma principles were proclaimed. The Pandya king is not named but shows Mauryan awareness of southern kingdoms.

q: The partition of Bengal was annulled in:
explain: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905. Due to massive protests (Swadeshi Movement), the partition was annulled in 1911 when the capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi.

q: India gained independence from British rule on:
explain: India gained independence on 15 August 1947. Jawaharlal Nehru became the first Prime Minister.

q: The Sun Temple at Konark was built by:
explain: Konark Sun Temple (Odisha, 13th century CE) was built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. Designed as a massive chariot with 24 wheels for the Sun God Surya.

q: 'Ettuthokai' means:
explain: Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies) is a collection of 8 Sangam-age anthologies of Tamil poetry: Ainkurunuru, Narrinai, Akananuru, Purananuru, Kalittokai, Kuruntokai, Patirruppattu, and Paripatal.

q: Lord Mountbatten announced the date of partition as:
explain: The Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) of 3 June 1947 announced the partition of British India into India and Pakistan. 15 August was set as the transfer of power date.

q:
With reference to the Russian Revolution of 1917, consider the following statements:
1. The February Revolution led to the abdication of Tsar Nicholas II.
2. The October Revolution, led by the Bolsheviks under Lenin, overthrew the Provisional Government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the February Revolution ended Tsarist rule, and the October Revolution (Bolshevik-led, under Lenin) then overthrew Kerensky's Provisional Government.

q: The decimal system of numeration was developed in:
explain: The decimal system with place value notation (including zero) was developed in India during the Gupta period, later transmitted to Arabs and then to Europe.

q: The greatest ruler of Vijayanagara Empire was:
explain: Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529 CE) was the greatest ruler — a brilliant military commander, poet (wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu), and generous patron of arts. Known as Kannada Rajya Rama Ramana.

q: The Purusha Sukta, which describes the creation of the four varnas, is in:
explain: The Purusha Sukta (Rigveda, 10th Mandala, Hymn 90) describes the cosmic being Purusha's sacrifice: Brahmins from his mouth, Kshatriyas from arms, Vaishyas from thighs, Shudras from feet.

q: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in:
explain: First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi using the Tulughma strategy and artillery, establishing the Mughal Empire in India.

q: The Gupta Empire is called the 'Golden Age' of India because:
opts: Great achievements in science, maths, art, and literature
It had the most gold reserves
explain: The Gupta period (320–550 CE) is called the Golden Age: Aryabhata discovered zero and calculated pi; Kalidasa wrote Shakuntala, Meghaduta; Varahamihira was an astronomer; Sushruta was a physician; the Nalanda university flourished.

q: The Upanishads deal with:
explain: The Upanishads (c. 800–200 BCE) are philosophical texts exploring the nature of ultimate reality (Brahman), individual soul (Atman), and their identity. They form the basis of Vedanta philosophy.

q: The first railway line in India ran between:
explain: India's first railway line ran between Bombay (Bori Bunder) and Thane on 16 April 1853, a distance of 34 km. The train pulled by three engines carried 400 passengers.

q: Aurangzeb's policy of destroying Hindu temples led to:
opts: Increased revolts by Rajputs, Marathas, Sikhs
explain: Aurangzeb's orthodox Islamic policies and temple destruction increased revolts by Rajputs, Marathas, and Sikhs, weakening the Mughal Empire.

q: The Mughal emperor famous for building Taj Mahal:
explain: Shah Jahan (1628-1658) built the Taj Mahal at Agra (1632-1643) as a mausoleum for his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which country was first to land humans on the Moon?
explain: USA's Apollo 11 mission (July 1969) was the first crewed lunar landing. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969. Armstrong was the first human to walk on the Moon.

q:
With reference to the Indian National Army (INA), consider the following statements:
1. It was reorganised under the leadership of Subhas Chandra Bose in 1943 with Japanese support.
2. The INA trials at the Red Fort (1945-46) generated widespread sympathy across India for the accused officers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — Bose reorganised the INA (Azad Hind Fauj) in 1943, and the subsequent Red Fort trials of INA officers sparked nationwide sympathy and protest.

q: The Battle of Plassey (1757) was fought between:
explain: The Battle of Plassey (1757) was fought between Robert Clive of the British East India Company and Nawab Siraj-ud-daulah of Bengal. British victory established colonial dominance.

q:
With reference to the Indus Valley Civilization, consider the following statements:
1. Lothal is the only Harappan site with an artificial dockyard.
2. Dholavira is located on the banks of the Indus river in present-day Punjab.
3. Kalibangan has yielded evidence of the world's earliest ploughed field.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Statement 1 is correct — Lothal (Gujarat) uniquely has a dockyard. Statement 2 is incorrect — Dholavira is in Gujarat (Rann of Kutch), not Punjab. Statement 3 is correct — Kalibangan (Rajasthan) shows the earliest known ploughed field. Hence 1 and 3 only.

q:
With reference to Mughal art and architecture, consider the following statements:
1. The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was built to commemorate Akbar's victory over Gujarat.
2. Miniature painting flourished under Mughal patronage, blending Persian and Indian styles.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the Buland Darwaza commemorates Akbar's Gujarat victory (1573), and Mughal miniature painting is a well-known Perso-Indian artistic synthesis.

q: The Ajanta Caves are famous for:
explain: Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra, 2nd century BCE – 7th century CE) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites famous for their magnificent Buddhist cave paintings and sculptures depicting Jataka stories.

q: The 'Lucknow Pact' (1916) was an agreement between:
explain: The Lucknow Pact (1916) was an agreement between the Indian National Congress (led by Tilak) and the All India Muslim League (led by Jinnah) for joint action against British rule and for separate electorates.

q: The three Sangam kingdoms (Muvendars) of ancient Tamil Nadu were:
explain: The three Muvendars (great kings) of the Sangam Age were: Cheras (capital: Vanji/Karur), Cholas (capital: Puhar/Kaveripattinam), and Pandyas (capital: Madurai). They ruled Tamil Nadu from c. 300 BCE to 300 CE.

q: Abdur Razzaq, the Persian ambassador, visited which Vijayanagara king's court?
explain: Abdur Razzaq (Persian envoy, 1443) visited the court of Devaraya II and gave a detailed description of Vijayanagara city and the empire's grandeur.

q: The partition of Bengal (1905) was done by:
explain: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal on 16 October 1905 (dividing along communal lines: West Bengal + Bihar + Orissa vs. East Bengal + Assam). This sparked massive nationalist protests and the Swadeshi Movement. Partition was revoked in 1911.

q: The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced:
explain: Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) introduced separate electorates for Muslims — Muslims would vote only for Muslim candidates — a communal step that sowed seeds of partition.

id: history-149-The Chola Empire was a f
q: The Chola Empire was a famous empire from which part of India?
explain: The Chola Empire was one of the longest-ruling dynasties in South India (Tamil Nadu), known for maritime power, temple architecture, and administration.

q: The Medieval Chola Empire was founded by:
explain: Vijayalaya Chola (c. 848 CE) founded the Medieval Chola dynasty by capturing Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyar (who were Pallava vassals). He built the first Nishumbhasudani temple at Thanjavur.

q: The Chipko Movement (1973) was related to:
explain: Chipko Movement (1973) in Uttarakhand was an environmental movement where villagers hugged trees to prevent them from being cut.

q: Harshavardhana's empire was described by the Chinese pilgrim:
explain: Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) visited India during Harsha's reign (7th century CE) and described Harsha's empire and character in detail in his 'Si-Yu-Ki' (Record of Western Countries).

q: Alauddin Khalji introduced market reforms to:
opts: Control prices to maintain a large army cheaply
explain: Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) introduced price control markets (Sarai Adl) to keep commodity prices fixed, enabling him to maintain a large army (3,00,000 cavalry) at low cost. Four regulated markets: grain, cattle, cloth, miscellaneous.

q: The famous rock-cut architecture of the Mauryan period includes:
opts: Barabar Caves (Bihar) — earliest rock-cut caves in India
explain: The Barabar Caves (Bihar) are the earliest surviving rock-cut caves in India, built during Ashoka's reign (c. 3rd century BCE) for the Ajivika sect. They have highly polished interiors (Mauryan polish).

q: Indian National Army's women's regiment was named:
explain: INA's women's regiment was the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, named after Rani Lakshmi Bai, commanded by Captain Lakshmi Sahgal (Dr. Lakshmi). About 1,500 women enlisted.

q: 'Swadeshi' movement was mainly a response to:
explain: The Swadeshi movement (1905-1908) was launched in response to the partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon. It promoted use of Indian goods and boycott of British products.

q: Akbar's 'Ain-i-Akbari' and 'Akbarnama' were written by:
explain: Abul Fazl (1551–1602), a minister and historian, wrote Akbarnama (in 3 volumes, including the Ain-i-Akbari). The Ain-i-Akbari is a detailed account of Akbar's administration, court, culture, and statistics of the empire.

q: Gautama Buddha was born at:
explain: Siddhartha Gautama was born c. 563 BCE at Lumbini (present-day Nepal) in the Shakya clan. His birth, enlightenment, first sermon, and Mahaparinirvana are the four most sacred events in Buddhism.

q: Ashokan pillars are made of:
explain: Ashokan pillars are made of a single piece of highly polished Chunar sandstone. The polish is so fine that they look like metal — technique still not fully understood.

q: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded by:
opts: Harihara I and Bukka Raya I
explain: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 CE by brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I (formerly commanders of the Kampili kingdom) with the spiritual guidance of sage Vidyaranya (Madhava). Capital: Hampi (Vijayanagara).

q: Kalibangan, an Indus Valley site, is located in:
explain: Kalibangan is located in Hanumangarh district, Rajasthan, on the Ghaggar (ancient Saraswati) river. Famous for fire altars, ploughed fields (earliest evidence of ploughing), and pre-Harappan settlement.

q: Bodhgaya is associated with:
explain: Bodhgaya (Bihar) is where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree and became the Buddha. It is the holiest Buddhist pilgrimage site.

q: Who is associated with the Green Revolution in India?
explain: Green Revolution in India is associated with M.S. Swaminathan (plant geneticist) and Minister C. Subramaniam.

q: The 'Hathigumpha inscription' of Kharavela provides information about which dynasty?
explain: The Hathigumpha (Elephant Cave) inscription near Bhubaneswar describes the achievements of Kharavela, the greatest king of the Chedi dynasty of Kalinga (1st century BCE).

q: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire with the help of:
explain: Chandragupta Maurya (322–297 BCE) founded the Mauryan Empire with the guidance of Chanakya (also known as Kautilya), the author of Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft.

q: The 'Champaran Satyagraha' (1917) was Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India against:
explain: Champaran Satyagraha (1917) in Bihar was Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India — against the tinkathia system forcing indigo cultivation on peasants. Gandhi's first major success in India.

q: The Pallava 'Pancha Rathas' (Five Chariots) at Mahabalipuram are:
opts: Five temples built for five Pandava brothers and Draupadi — monolithic rock-cut structures
Stone chariots imported from North India
explain: The Pancha Rathas (Arjuna, Bhima, Dharmaraja/Yudhishthira, Nakula-Sahadeva, Draupadi Rathas) at Mahabalipuram are monolithic rock-cut structures carved from a single rock. They are incomplete and were never used as temples.

q: Gautama Buddha attained enlightenment at:
explain: Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment (Nirvana) at Bodh Gaya under the Bodhi Tree.

q: Who gave the slogan 'Jai Hind'?
explain: 'Jai Hind' (Victory to India) was given as a rallying cry by Subhas Chandra Bose, head of the Indian National Army (INA). It became India's national salutation.

q: The standard unit of weight used by the Harappans was:
opts: Based on the binary system (doubling: 1,2,4,8,16,32,64) and then decimal
explain: Harappan weights followed a binary system up to 64, then decimal: 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,160,200,320,640. Cuboid chert weights were found across sites, suggesting standardised trade.

q:
With reference to early Indian nationalist organisations before the Congress, consider the following statements:
1. The Indian Association was founded by Surendranath Banerjee in 1876.
2. The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was founded in Maharashtra to voice public grievances to the government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the Indian Association (Calcutta, 1876) under Surendranath Banerjee, and the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) were significant pre-Congress political organisations.

q: The Dandi March (Salt Satyagraha) was in:
explain: Gandhi started the Dandi March (Salt March) on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, defying the salt tax.

q: The 'Shore Temple' at Mahabalipuram was built by:
explain: The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) was built by Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) in the early 8th century CE. It is one of the oldest structural stone temples in South India.

q: The Hazara Rama Temple in Hampi was built by:
explain: Hazara Rama Temple (Temple of 1000 Ramas) in Hampi was built during the reign of Krishnadevaraya, known for its magnificent bas-reliefs depicting scenes from the Ramayana.

q: Badami was the capital of:
explain: Badami (Vatapi) in Karnataka was the capital of the Chalukyas of Badami (Western Chalukyas, 543-753 CE), who created magnificent rock-cut cave temples there.

q: Which Sangam text is known as 'Tamil Bible'?
explain: Tirukkural by Tiruvalluvar is often called 'Tamil Bible' or 'Universal Veda' for its universal wisdom on virtue, wealth, and love applicable to all humanity.

q: The first Sultan of Delhi was:
explain: Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210 CE) was the first Sultan of Delhi and founder of the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty. He was a slave of Muhammad Ghori. He started the Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque.

q: Gayatri Mantra is found in:
explain: Gayatri Mantra (dedicated to solar deity Savitri) is found in the Rigveda (3.62.10). It is the most sacred mantra in Hinduism.

q:
Match List-I (event) with List-II (year) and select the correct answer:

List-I
A. States Reorganisation Act (linguistic states)
B. Sino-Indian War
C. Indo-Pak War leading to creation of Bangladesh
D. Green Revolution's major early impact in Punjab/Haryana

List-II
1. 1971
2. 1956
3. 1962
4. Late 1960s
explain: States Reorganisation Act (1956); Sino-Indian War (1962); 1971 Indo-Pak War creating Bangladesh; Green Revolution's early major impact in Punjab/Haryana from the late 1960s. Correct: A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4.

q: The famous Chola king of the Sangam age who completed the Red Canal (Kallanai/Grand Anicut) was:
explain: Karikalan (Karikala Chola, c. 1st–2nd century CE) was the most famous Sangam Chola. He built the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) across the Kaveri river — the oldest surviving dam in the world (still in use today).

q: The Battle of Plassey (1757) gave the British control over:
explain: The Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757): Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah (Bengal Nawab) with the help of traitor Mir Jafar. This gave the EIC control over Bengal — beginning British colonial rule in India.

q: The 'Grand Trunk Road' was built by:
explain: Grand Trunk Road from Chittagong to Kabul was built/renovated by Sher Shah Suri (16th century). Originally an ancient road, Sher Shah restored and extended it, planting trees and building sarais.

q: The invasion of Timur (Tamerlane) devastated Delhi in:
explain: Timur (Tamerlane) of Samarkand invaded India and sacked Delhi in 1398 CE, massacring 100,000+ prisoners and looting enormous wealth. This destroyed the Tughlaq dynasty and led to the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties.

q: The Lahore Resolution (1940) demanding Pakistan was passed by:
opts: Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah
explain: The Lahore Resolution (23 March 1940) — also called the Pakistan Resolution — was passed by the All-India Muslim League. It demanded separate independent states for Muslim-majority areas in northwest and northeast India. Jinnah gave the Two-Nation Theory.

q: The Chishti Silsila of Sufi order in India was founded by:
explain: Moinuddin Chishti (1142-1236 CE) brought the Chishti order to India, establishing his khanqah at Ajmer. He and his followers emphasized love of God and service.

q: The Green Revolution in India aimed at:
explain: Green Revolution (1960s-70s) aimed to increase agricultural production (wheat, rice) through high-yielding varieties and modern techniques.

q: The Ghadar Party was founded by:
explain: Ghadar Party was founded in 1913 at San Francisco by Sohan Singh Bhakna (president) and Lala Hardayal (Secretary) among Indian immigrants to organize a mutiny against British rule.

q: The Rowlatt Act (1919) gave the British power to:
explain: Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed British to imprison any person without trial for up to 2 years.

q: The Dravidian Movement in Tamil Nadu was influenced significantly by which organization?
explain: The Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation, 1916) was the forerunner of the Dravidian movement. It championed non-Brahmin rights and eventually evolved into the Dravidian parties.

q: The first woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate was:
explain: Razia Sultana (1236-1240 CE), daughter of Iltutmish, was the first woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. She discarded purdah and held court openly.

q: Which Buddhist council was held during the reign of Ashoka?
explain: The 3rd Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra (c. 250 BCE) under the patronage of Emperor Ashoka, presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa. The Pali Canon (Tipitaka) was finalised here.
